speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We would also like to express our thanks to the House, to the Government and to all our fellow Parliamentarians for your patience, for your generosity.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Thirty seconds have gone by and have been lost.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We are familiar with art when it is "art".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We understand them sometimes as something material, like a painting, sculpture, an installation, or an event over a specific time, like a performance or movie screening.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We are familiar with these arts being produced and presented in conventional spaces, such as a theatre, gallery spaces, cinemas, screening rooms, studios and so on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Of course, there are occasions when these works are presented in alternative spaces.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: But there are also defined spaces, like in a church, in a quarry or in a cemetery.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: These are privately managed public spaces, providing focused spaces for developing and appreciating artistic expression.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: They congregate audiences and supporters of the arts, therefore, creating also a sense of community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: They have become iconic sites and attractions in their own right, not only for locals, but also for visitors from the region and abroad who are interested in finding out what our artistic community is doing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: But art is not just what occurs in these spaces.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Human capacity for expression is not limited to just these spaces.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Art is not just artifice – which it also can be – it is also about life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When artists take art beyond conventional spaces, they seek to engage with the expressions of the everyday and in sites of the everyday.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Here, the gestures and relationships of our everyday spaces and activities become the material of art.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Art as life helps us to understand ourselves, allows us to reinvent ourselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When art happens in everyday places, the space and the gesture, the expression, all become a curio.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: This distancing, what we call an aesthetic distancing, stimulates queries, investigation, reflections and, on many occasions, even actions, to realise the reinvention.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It comes with some inconvenience, but necessary to stimulate our creative and imaginative being.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: As I have said before, creativity comes from ruptures, from interventions, from challenging norms, perceived notions and habits.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And when such art practices happen in everyday spaces, it becomes all the more immediate, because everyday places are public spaces that allow people to interact and be in communal engagement with one another.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: As a small nation city, we have quite a substantial population, we have a lot of built-up areas – flats, huge shopping centres, office buildings.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And with so much focus on economic and consumeristic activities and successes, public spaces for everyday interaction and communal engagement are important.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: As Peter G Rowe, a Professor at Harvard University’s Graduate School of Design said, “  makes me feel as though I’m part of a human race, not the rat race!” When familiar everyday space is filled with excitement and surprises, one becomes rejuvenated and excited.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: One becomes attentive to things around us, not taking them for granted.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Hence, art as life, in everyday places, is one important way to reconnect to our spontaneity, to rediscover our curiosity, to repair our relationships with space, things and people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Now, I will talk about permits and permission related to the use of this space.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: But first, let me recall my early years when I was working at The Substation, founded by Mr Kuo Pao Kun.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: By the way, today is the 16th death anniversary of Mr Kuo.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The Substation is also called "The Home for the Arts".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And, indeed, it is a home for many artists and many different arts practices.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There was this sense of free spirit where conversations flow, things happen.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It is a place that celebrates spontaneity, respects artists and their work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It also respects audience by honouring them as individuals who are generous even when they may have different tastes in and preferences on art.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: On a busy night, there would be a set-up in the garden to prep for a performance or a hard rock gig with very noisy sound tests.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There will be people after watching a piece of theatre in the Black Box, they will be gathering in the Garden, discussing what they saw, debating what they liked or disliked, expressing their frustration over some impenetrable work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In the same Garden, artists like Zai Kuning, Tang Da Wu, Amanda Heng, or academics like Lai Ah Eng would be at the Garden, probably talking to one another after a conference, while some people may be practising on their guitars, or basker Roy Payamal would be practising his juggling skill in the Garden.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Street performing artist Roy did not need to ask permission to practise at the Garden.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Roy made sure that whenever his juggling ball flew out of his hand, crossing the path of anyone there, he would pick it up and, in his very gentle manner, would smile apologetically.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Why did I take such pain to describe The Substation Garden?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Because it was here that I learnt about what makes a space, a place and what makes a good public space.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Here, I learnt to debate, to listen, to know that there are so many art forms, so many possible artistic practices, so many different opinions that it is important not to judge, but to know that we are all different – we have different opinions and we can co-exist.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That is why it became such an amazing public space for artists and audience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And I do not remember me, being an arts administrator there managing the Garden, having to do any policing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Now, on the point of permits and permission, within conventional spaces, certain conditions of the space and use may already determine how art is developed or presented.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I have to say that it is to the credit of some of these public arts institutions, like the Esplanade, National Gallery, which have gone the extra mile to reach out to audiences to place-make these public spaces.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: However, would these huge public institutions, where artists gather, where artists would meet and talk about ideas, allow people to be spontaneous?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: What if when dancers, while discussing their future work at the foyer, start to move to demonstrate ideas, then followed by some improvisations that come along in response to the movements?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I have checked with some of the artists and there are stories where they told me that they would be stopped by the security guards.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And the reasons cited would be that such activities or behaviour would create disturbances to other visitors.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Have we become over-zealous in our effort to make sure that these public spaces are well kept, thereby taking away the spirit of spontaneity of an artistic space?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, how can these privately owned public institutions allow such spontaneity?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: What about the use of everyday spaces for the arts?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There are permits and laws that prohibit certain kinds of activities or expressions, such as the Public Order Act, Public Disturbance, Obscenity Act, and so on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: These laws do articulate to an extent, and to a measure of certainty and interpretation, the scope of what is legal or permitted by the authorities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: On a weekday night, a musician outside Toa Payoh Library – you know there is big square there – practising his guitar.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: His skill was so good that he attracted people gathering around him.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: He responded because it was fun and he asked them to start to move and dance.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: People may say that this is a hypothetical situation and Singaporeans are not so spontaneous.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I disagree because after many years of artistic practices in public spaces, I find that Singaporeans want to tell their stories.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: They want to express and connect with artists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That desire is innate, deeply human, to be with one another, to do things spontaneously.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In the early years of our forum theatre performances, we had to beg people to come up to make interventions or to expect our friends to come up to make interventions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When we set up tables for conversations on end-of-life issues, people would sit and share and will not stop until we tell them that we have to end by 10.00 pm, because that is stipulated in our performance licence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Yet, I also would agree that Singaporeans are not so spontaneous because I think we have been culturally and politically conditioned to be cautious.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Deputy Speaker, there are a lot of instances where art works well in public and everyday spaces.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In one of our recent works, THE LESSON, which talked about how one makes difficult choices on land issues and what is a democratic process, people stayed to participate, debate and are respectful of one another.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Crowd events, such as Night Fest and so on, where there certainly is not a high ratio of security for the crowd it attracts, would go on peacefully.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I would say that the populace knows how to experience and understand art in these places.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Can art happen beyond the 30 places prescribed by the Government?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Only when art can happen in ordinary and everyday places, then can we claim, as in the Arts and Culture Strategic Review (ACSR) report, that art is everywhere.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Then there is still the question of what kind of work is permitted and who can decide on them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In the case of artistic expression, is it (a) aesthetic, which can be subjective; (b) moral, which has a level of subjectivity, too, and which has certain aspects covered under legal terms; or (c) political, which should be distinguished from legal?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: What are all these considerations that help decide if that work can be done in public or in everyday spaces?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: What if there was a case where an artistic expression does not flout the law?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Should or can it then be permissible by default?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Or if permission were sought for such an artistic expression that does not flout the law, would it be granted?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Would it also be allowed if it is done without applying for a permit and licence?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It is a quiet piece; it does not create any disturbances; it is performance art in the public.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: What if there are some complaints from certain members of the public to the work?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Does it then mean that it should be taken down, or the performance being stopped?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Can an individual or a group who disagrees with a particular artistic work or message then advocate for it to be removed in the name of it being in the public space?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The right to a city, this is an idea proposed by French sociologist Henri Lebefreve who talks about, if a city, which also includes the public space, is meant for the public, it should be safe and permissible for everyone to be there, to interact, to exchange information and ideas, as long as the exchange does not incinerate and create disorder.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That is a right to the city, a right for everyone.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, what should we do if there are complaints about artistic work being placed in a public space?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Unfortunately, much of our cultural development is currently perceived as being directed 'top-down'.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: This is how public spaces should be managed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It is about dialogues, sometimes with disagreement, but the intention is to include, not to exclude.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I hope that this Government would trust that artists in Singapore are very responsible people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: A lot of times, when they make work, they do works that are personal with a lot of committed beliefs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When we talk about earning trust, it is not just about sitting there and say, "Hey, show me you can be trusted".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It means one needs to reach out to connect in order to express trust.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The public space, being a space where strangers meet strangers, means we have to be able to trust by connecting and not by segregating or being territorial or tribal.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Any honest and truthful artist works on trust.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Because without which they would not put their artworks in the public to be critiqued, to be judged.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: An artwork is a personal and deep expression of self.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And to show it to the public, one must trust the audience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It is this gesture of faith in our capacity as artists, as human beings, that we want to reach out to people and to hear and get their response.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Likewise, I hope the audience, the public, the Government, everyone, would have the same faith in the artists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Art practices in everyday spaces are an expression of this trust and this connection.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I am glad I did not have to guillotine you.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister for Culture, Community and Youth Grace Fu.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun referred to the many opportunities for art in public spaces beyond the conventional gallery, theatre or studio.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In fact, he has mentioned several examples of how forum theatre has been able to engage the public in multiple locations in Singapore, having good engagement on topics that can be difficult, emotional and sensitive at times.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: That is, in fact, the best testament of how art has been able to be carried out in public with trust, with good conversations and mutual understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, I am glad that he is, indeed, affirming that this has taken place in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Kok also noted that the Singapore Night Festival organised by the National Heritage Board (NHB) has done well to balance accessibility and security.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I agree with Mr Kok that Singapore’s arts and culture scene, including art in our public spaces, is, indeed, vibrant and thriving.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Aside from the Night Festival, there are many, many other opportunities for Singaporeans to enjoy art in everyday spaces in the city centre, as well as in our heartlands.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These include NHB’s Singapore Heritage Festival, National Gallery Singapore’s Light to Night, the National Arts Council’s (NAC’s) Arts in Your Neighbourhood, and People Association's (PA’s) PAssionArts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Kok also spoke about the spaces that are currently available for public art.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under NAC’s Busking Scheme, over 250 buskers have been endorsed since 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They include the father and son duo, Mr Mashruddin Saharuddin and Nizaruddin, who were featured at this year’s National Day Parade, and whose performances have enlivened city life and energised urban spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am pleased to update that NAC has secured over 50 sites around Singapore for public art, from a shophouse wall in Boat Quay to an open area near a Housing and Development Board (HDB) block in Tampines.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NAC will continue to identify more of such spaces, and work with site owners to make them available for artists to showcase their work.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together with spaces for street art at Goodman Arts Centre, Aliwal Arts Centre, and *SCAPE, these sites will help augment our arts and cultural offerings and add vibrancy to our city.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MCCY remains committed to making the arts and culture accessible to everyone, and to working closely in partnership with arts practitioners as well as enthusiasts, hobbyists and volunteers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We want to create an environment where more Singaporeans, and not only trained artists, can appreciate and participate in the arts, so that the arts are an integral part of all our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At this year's PAssionArts Festival in July and August, a memorable experience was the Animal Art workshop where three-generational families and neighbours came together to create and paint on wooden planks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And this is an example of how art in everyday spaces, in everyday places, and in everyday lives, can help build the connections which Mr Kok referred to, and which my Ministry also seeks to develop among Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are also stepping up efforts to engage our youths who are the future generations of artists, patrons and supporters of the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To do this, we provide opportunities for talented youths to showcase their work.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the recent Night Festival, I had the pleasure of interacting with two groups involving students from the Singapore University of Technology and Design and their work – Hyperbands by Kopi/O and Orbit by LiteWerkz.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Their enthusiasm demonstrated how we must continue to support our youths in pursuing their passions, including by expressing themselves and showcasing a part of our Singaporean identity through the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government supports art in everyday spaces because we are aware of its ability to shape common experiences and to spark shared interests.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And if done well, this can help Singaporeans develop stronger bonds and bring us together as a people.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the same time, however, we are mindful that our public spaces serve a wide range of needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We need to be sensitive and respectful of the different perspectives, values and way of life in our multicultural and multigenerational society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is MCCY's role to ensure that we promote the arts and raise arts excellence in a way that gains strong public support for arts and culture across the board.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Therefore, in promoting public art, we must strike a careful balance between the artists and the stakeholders who own and use the premises.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, park users may appreciate the occasional band performance but prefer to keep the park quiet and serene at other times.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Therein lies the need to consult different stakeholders as a matter of respect and basic courtesy – those who own and use the space should also have a say.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am sure that Mr Kok Heng Leun can see the merits of this approach, as he has often advocated for acknowledging diversity in views, in this case from different users of public spaces, including non-arts practitioners.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: He, too, has noted the importance of how public art should not flout the law or create public disorder.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, the Government, through NAC, commissions key public art works.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The first three commissions under the Public Art Trust (PAT) were conceived to commemorate Singapore's Golden Jubilee.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In other words, we are actively supporting, financing and cultivating artists to bring public artworks, sculptures and installation art to public spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NAC has made efforts to involve the arts community in good public art projects through its grants.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Open House, a recipient of NAC's Major Company Scheme funding, curates art walks that bring art into unexpected, everyday spaces, such as HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, the success of the arts in Singapore is the result of a strong and mutually beneficial partnership among the Government, the corporates and individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NAC not only encourages private donations for new public art, but also engages key partners for their support, such as in securing new sites for this art.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, the PAT advises both site owners and artists on best practices in commissioning, installing, maintaining and decommissioning public artworks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, to present public art that is relevant to Singaporeans from all communities and walks of life, we must continue to bring art closer to the community through thoughtful programming and outreach.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The initiatives of our arts groups, like the national orchestras and Mr Kok's own Drama Box, in the heartlands are good examples.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The PAT commissioned a Stop and Smell the Ang Mo Dan! exhibition with NAC's Arts In Your Neighbourhood initiative in March this year.
